I asked an AI to resolve Makeev's conjecture for some dimension $d>3$: Let $\pm v_1,\ldots,\pm v_n\in\mathbb R^d$ ($d>3$) be vectors of the $A_d$ root system, where $n=d(d+1)/2$. These are the vectors $\{e_i-e_j:i\ne j\}\subset\{x\in\mathbb R^{d+1}:\sum_{i=0}^d x_i=0\}\cong\mathbb R^d$. The AI produced some partial results in part1.txt, and a counterexample in dimension 4 in part2.txt. (These are copied from the AI chat window.) Please check if there are any errors in the proof.

1. The background can mostly be replaced by Kuperberg

Kuperberg already establishes:

  • the equivalence between constant-width bodies and odd functions on the sphere;

  • the equivalence between circumscription by the dual difference body of a simplex and linearity of an odd function on a rotated Ad​ root system;

  • the test-bundle formulation;

  • the nonzero Euler-class argument in dimension 3;

  • the vanishing of that primary obstruction in dimensions d≥4.

Thus the historical and bundle-theoretic portion can be reduced to approximately one paragraph:

Kuperberg showed that Makeev’s constant-width-body conjecture is equivalent to the assertion that every continuous odd function on Sd−1 agrees with a linear function on a rotated Ad​ root system. He proved the assertion in dimension 3 by a nonzero Euler-class calculation and showed that the same Euler-class obstruction vanishes in dimensions d≥4, leaving the higher-dimensional geometric question undecided.

That accurately summarizes the prior literature without reconstructing the bundle. NYJM

The explicit normalized coordinates

uij​=2​ei​−ej​​

should still be retained, because all subsequent calculations depend on that normalization.

2. The exact-label lemma is standard graph Hodge theory

The exact-label space is the cut or gradient space of the complete graph Kd+1​. The space

C={X:XT=−X, X1=0}

is its orthogonal complement, the divergence-free cycle space.

In cochain language:

  • c is a 0-cochain;

  • yij​=(ci​−cj​)/2​ is its coboundary;

  • the triangle sum

    yij​+yjk​+yki​

    is the combinatorial curl;

  • because the clique complex of the complete graph is a simplex and has H1=0, curl-free 1-cochains are exact;

  • the orthogonal complement of the gradients is the divergence-free space.

This is precisely the complete-graph specialization of the combinatorial Hodge/Helmholtz decomposition. Jiang–Lim–Yao–Ye explicitly formulate gradient edge flows, divergence-free flows, triangle curl, and the fact that on a complete graph triangular consistency implies global consistency. arXiv+1

I would nevertheless keep a four-line direct proof, because the formula

ci​=2​yi0​

makes the result completely transparent. The literature citation should replace the dimension-count discussion and supply terminology, not make the paper less self-contained.

Most importantly, Part 2 should not repeat the entire lemma. Its matrix condition

is merely the same decomposition in the m=5 model. The two current versions occupy substantial space.

A concise combined statement would be:

For a skew edge matrix Y, the following are equivalent:

Yij​=ρi​−ρj​,Yij​+Yjk​+Yki​=0,ΠYΠ=0.

Equivalently, Y is orthogonal to every skew matrix X with X1=0.

4. The C0-stability proof can cite local degree theory

The calculation

DTp​(I)=−2​3​I

must remain. It is the substantive local fact.

After that, the rest can be compressed to:

Since 0 is a nondegenerate zero of Tp​, its local Brouwer degree is ±1. Nonzero local degree persists under sufficiently small uniform perturbations. Since

∥Tf​−Tp​∥∞​≤(2d+1​)​∥f−p∥∞​,

every sufficiently small C0 perturbation of p has a zero of its test map.

The current boundary-ball and straight-line homotopy argument is correct but is essentially the proof of this standard local-degree stability theorem. Brouwer degree is specifically designed to obtain existence and persistence under uniform rather than differentiable perturbations. Springer

An inverse-function-theorem citation alone would not be an adequate replacement: it would naturally give stability under C1 perturbations of the test map, whereas the theorem asserts stability under C0 perturbations of f.

5. The final perturbation argument has a short abstract form

The sequential compactness proof in part 2 is valid, but it can be replaced by the following reusable lemma.

Compact obstruction lemma

Let M be compact, let E be finite-dimensional, and let

F0​,F1​:M⟶E

be continuous. Suppose that there is a continuous family

λx​∈E∗

such that

λx​(F0​(x))=0for every x∈M,(A)

and

F0​(x)=0⟹λx​(F1​(x))=0.(B)

Then there is ε0​>0 such that

F0​(x)+εF1​(x)=0

for every x∈M and every 0<∣ε∣<ε0​.

Proof

Let Z=F0−1​(0). By compactness and (B), there is a neighborhood U of Z on which

λx​(F1​(x))=0.

On the compact set M∖U,

a:=M∖Umin​∥F0​∥>0.

Also let B=maxM​∥F1​∥. For ∣ε∣<a/B, the sum cannot vanish on M∖U. If it vanished at x∈U, then applying λx​ and using (A) would give

0=ελx​(F1​(x)),

a contradiction. ∎

Apply this with

M=SO(4),F0​=TQ​,F1​=TH​,

and with λg​ induced by Λg​. Lemma 3 is condition (A), and Lemma 4 is condition (B). This replaces all of Section 5 by one paragraph. The current sequential version appears at the end of part 2.

Karasev’s counterexample to a different Knaster-like conjecture of Makeev uses a genuinely similar pattern: introduce small geometric parameters, assume solutions persist, pass by compactness to a limiting configuration, and obtain an infinitesimal condition deliberately violated by the chosen function. It is worth citing as methodological precedent, although the actual obstruction is different. arXiv

This is the part that remains.

Lemma 4 proves the highly specific statement

TQ​(g)=0⟹Λg​(YH​(g))=0

for the particular cubic Q, quintic H, simplex, and functional Λg​.

The following standard tools do not replace it:

  • generic transversality;

  • Palais-type symmetric criticality;

  • the Euler-class calculation;

  • general forced-symmetry-breaking theory;

  • ordinary representation-theoretic disjointness;

  • standard tensor diagonalization.

Those theories explain why a transverse perturbation is plausible, but they do not prove that this explicit quintic is nonzero at every cubic zero.

Comparison with Chen’s representation-theoretic argument

Chen’s 2026 argument for the regular dodecahedron is the closest recent model. It uses an A5​-equivariant evaluation map and the fact that degree-3 harmonics and linear functions have no common irreducible A5​-summands. Schur’s lemma therefore forces both sides of a putative equality to vanish. arXiv

That shortcut is unavailable for the A4​ simplex. Let V4​ denote the standard 4-dimensional representation of A5​. A character calculation using the same A5​ table gives

Eexact​≅V4​,

and

C≅Λ2V4​≅V3​⊕V3′​.

Meanwhile,

H3​(R4)​≅Sym3(V4​)⊖V4​≅1⊕V3​⊕V3′​⊕V4​⊕V5​.​

Thus every representation type occurring in the exact-label and cycle spaces already occurs in the harmonic cubics. There is no irreducible-component mismatch that can force the cycle defect to vanish.

Representation theory can still improve the exposition:

  • the tangent space to the orbit of p is

    Tp​(SO(4)⋅p)≅V3​⊕V3′​;

  • cubic exactness means Q∘g lies in its normal space

    1⊕V4​⊕V5​;

  • Lemma 4 is then a statement about a particular quintic functional on that critical locus.

But the critical locus still has to be classified, or the nonvanishing still has to be proved by some equivalent calculation. I found no published result that performs that classification.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Independent symbolic checks for the algebra in part2.txt.

Requires SymPy.  The script verifies:
  * the seven-wedge expansion (54), modulo the stated exact term;
  * the associativity equations (E1)--(E8) from the multiplication table (34);
  * the formula (56)--(57) for Sigma and B_raw;
  * the resultant factorizations (45)--(46);
  * the simplification (59) and the three nonzero case values (60)--(62).
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Dict, List, Tuple

import sympy as sp


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Verify the edge expansion (54).
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
ai, aj, Ai, Aj, Bi, Bj = sp.symbols("ai aj Ai Aj Bi Bj")


def wedge(ui, uj, vi, vj):
    return sp.expand(ui * vj - vi * uj)


edge = sp.expand((ai - aj) ** 3 * (Ai - Aj) * (Bi - Bj))
formula_54 = (
    wedge(Bi, Bj, ai**3 * Ai, aj**3 * Aj)
    + wedge(Ai, Aj, ai**3 * Bi, aj**3 * Bj)
    - wedge(Ai * Bi, Aj * Bj, ai**3, aj**3)
    + 3 * wedge(ai, aj, ai**2 * Ai * Bi, aj**2 * Aj * Bj)
    - 3 * wedge(ai * Bi, aj * Bj, ai**2 * Ai, aj**2 * Aj)
    - 3 * wedge(ai * Ai, aj * Aj, ai**2 * Bi, aj**2 * Bj)
    + 3 * wedge(ai * Ai * Bi, aj * Aj * Bj, ai**2, aj**2)
)
exact_term = ai**3 * Ai * Bi - aj**3 * Aj * Bj
assert sp.expand(edge - formula_54 - exact_term) == 0


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Build the five-dimensional coordinatewise algebra from table (34).
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
ONE, a, b, A, B = range(5)
t, m, n, N, ell, Ell, v, V, k, K = sp.symbols(
    "t m n N ell Ell v V k K", commutative=True
)

Vector = List[sp.Expr]


def zero() -> Vector:
    return [sp.Integer(0)] * 5


def basis(i: int) -> Vector:
    out = zero()
    out[i] = sp.Integer(1)
    return out


def vector(**kwargs) -> Vector:
    names = {"one": ONE, "a": a, "b": b, "A": A, "B": B}
    out = zero()
    for name, value in kwargs.items():
        out[names[name]] = sp.sympify(value)
    return out


products: Dict[Tuple[int, int], Vector] = {}


def set_product(i: int, j: int, value: Vector) -> None:
    products[tuple(sorted((i, j)))] = value


for i, name in enumerate(("one", "a", "b", "A", "B")):
    set_product(ONE, i, vector(**{name: 1}))

set_product(a, A, vector(one=sp.Rational(2, 5), b=t, B=t))
set_product(b, B, vector(one=sp.Rational(2, 5), b=-t, B=-t))
set_product(a, a, vector(b=m / 2, A=n / 2, B=ell))
set_product(A, A, vector(B=m / 2, a=N / 2, b=Ell))
set_product(a, B, vector(a=t, b=N / 4, A=m / 2))
set_product(A, b, vector(A=t, B=n / 4, a=m / 2))
set_product(a, b, vector(a=t, A=ell, B=v / 2))
set_product(A, B, vector(A=t, a=Ell, b=V / 2))
set_product(b, b, vector(a=n / 4, b=-t, A=v / 2, B=k / 2))
set_product(B, B, vector(A=N / 4, B=-t, a=V / 2, b=K / 2))


def add(x: Vector, y: Vector) -> Vector:
    return [sp.expand(xi + yi) for xi, yi in zip(x, y)]


def scale(c, x: Vector) -> Vector:
    return [sp.expand(c * xi) for xi in x]


def multiply(x: Vector, y: Vector) -> Vector:
    out = zero()
    for i, xi in enumerate(x):
        if xi == 0:
            continue
        for j, yj in enumerate(y):
            if yj == 0:
                continue
            out = add(out, scale(xi * yj, products[tuple(sorted((i, j)))]))
    return [sp.expand(z) for z in out]


E = [basis(i) for i in range(5)]


def difference(x: Vector, y: Vector) -> Vector:
    return [sp.factor(z) for z in add(x, scale(-1, y))]


# The exact coefficient identities stated as E1--E8.
E1 = 3 * m * n - 4 * t * v
E2 = N * v + 16 * ell * t + 8 * m * t

assoc_2 = difference(multiply(multiply(E[a], E[b]), E[b]), multiply(E[a], multiply(E[b], E[b])))

assoc_3 = difference(multiply(multiply(E[a], E[a]), E[A]), multiply(E[a], multiply(E[a], E[A])))

assoc_5 = difference(multiply(multiply(E[a], E[b]), E[B]), multiply(E[a], multiply(E[b], E[B])))

def power(x: Vector, exponent: int) -> Vector:
    out = E[ONE]
    for _ in range(exponent):

def dot(x: Vector, y: Vector):
    # Sum of coordinates equals five times the coefficient of the all-ones vector.
    return sp.expand(5 * multiply(x, y)[ONE])


def wedge_pair(u: Vector, w: Vector, x: Vector, y: Vector):
    return sp.expand(dot(u, x) * dot(w, y) - dot(u, y) * dot(w, x))

    (1, vB, multiply(power(va, 3), vA)),
    (1, vA, multiply(power(va, 3), vB)),
    (-1, multiply(vA, vB), power(va, 3)),
    (3, va, multiply(multiply(power(va, 2), vA), vB)),
    (-3, multiply(va, vB), multiply(power(va, 2), vA)),
    (-3, multiply(va, vA), multiply(power(va, 2), vB)),
    (3, multiply(multiply(va, vA), vB), power(va, 2)),
]

Sigma = sp.Integer(0)
for coefficient, u0, w0 in terms:
    Sigma += sp.I * sp.Rational(1, 2) * coefficient * wedge_pair(vA, va, u0, w0)
    Sigma += sp.I * coefficient * wedge_pair(vB, vb, u0, w0)
Sigma = sp.expand(Sigma)

B_raw = (
    -960 * K * ell * t
    + 160 * Ell * ell * m
    + 320 * ell * t**2
    - 120 * m**3
    - 75 * m * N * n
    - 800 * m * t**2
    + 100 * m * V * v
    + 192 * m
    - 160 * n * t * V
)
assert sp.factor(Sigma + sp.I * B_raw / 80) == 0


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Verify the elimination in Case III.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
q, h, sigma = sp.symbols("q h sigma", real=True)
f43 = 3 * h * q**2 + 32 * q**2 - 448 * sigma * q - 256
f44 = -9 * h * q - 8 * sigma * h + 112 * sigma * q**2 - 96 * q

resultant_plus = sp.factor(sp.resultant(f43.subs(sigma, 1), f44.subs(sigma, 1), h))
resultant_minus = sp.factor(sp.resultant(f43.subs(sigma, -1), f44.subs(sigma, -1), h))
assert sp.factor(resultant_plus / (16 * (q - 4) * (q + 2) * (21 * q**2 + 42 * q + 16))) == 1
assert sp.factor(resultant_minus / (-16 * (q + 4) * (q - 2) * (21 * q**2 - 42 * q + 16))) == 1


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Verify the simplification (59) and the three case evaluations.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
abs_n2, abs_v2 = sp.symbols("abs_n2 abs_v2", real=True)
B_after_58 = (
    -960 * ell * (ell * m + 4 * t**2)
    + 160 * ell**2 * m
    + 320 * ell * t**2
    - 120 * m**3
    - 75 * m * abs_n2
    - 800 * m * t**2
    + 100 * m * abs_v2
    + 192 * m
    - 120 * m * abs_n2
)
B_59 = m * (180 * m**2 + 105 * abs_n2 - 4400 * t**2 - 128) - 3520 * ell * t**2

# Eliminate |n|^2 and |v|^2 using E6 and E8, with ell real.
abs_v2_expr = (8 - 20 * ell**2 - 60 * t**2) / 5
abs_n2_expr = (8 - 20 * ell**2 - 5 * m**2 + 40 * t**2) / 5
assert sp.factor(
    (B_after_58 - B_59).subs({abs_v2: abs_v2_expr, abs_n2: abs_n2_expr})
) == 0

# Case I.
assert sp.factor(B_59.subs({t: 0, abs_n2: 0, ell: 0, m**2: sp.Rational(8, 5)}) - 160 * m) == 0

# Case II.
assert sp.factor(
    B_59.subs({t**2: sp.Rational(1, 20), abs_n2: 0, ell: -m / 2, m**2: 1}) + 80 * m
) == 0

# Case III.
r = sp.sqrt(105)
q2 = (1 - r / 21) ** 2
h_value = (-74 + 14 * r) / 3
t2_value = 7 * (5 * r - 33) / 1440
ell_over_m = -(32 + 3 * h_value) / 64
case_iii_coefficient = sp.simplify(
    180 * q2 * t2_value
    + 105 * h_value * t2_value
    - 4400 * t2_value
    - 128
    - 3520 * ell_over_m * t2_value
)
assert sp.simplify(case_iii_coefficient - 60 * (75 - 7 * r)) == 0

print("All symbolic checks passed.")

\title[Makeev's root-system problem in dimension four]
{Makeev's $A_d$-root-system problem:\\a dimension-four counterexample}
\date{August 2026}

\begin{document}

\begin{abstract}
Let $u_{ij}=(e_i-e_j)/\sqrt2$ be the normalized roots of $A_d$ in
$V=\one^\perp\subset\R^{d+1}$.  We consider the assertion that every smooth
odd $f\colon S(V)\to\R$ agrees with a linear functional on some rotated copy
of all the roots $u_{ij}$.  We give a streamlined proof that the assertion is
false for $d=4$.  In the identification $\R^4\cong\C^2$, the counterexamples
are the small nonzero perturbations
\[
  f_\eps(z_1,z_2)
  =\Rea(z_1^2\overline{z_2})
   +\eps |z_1|^2\Ima(z_1^2\overline{z_2}).
\]
The proof is organized around two reusable statements: a gradient identity
for cubic edge labels and a compact obstruction lemma.  The only substantial
case-specific input is an explicit algebraic transversality proposition; its
coefficient calculation is isolated in an appendix.  We also record three
positive results from the same framework: the assertion holds for every odd
cubic plus a linear function, on a nonempty $C^0$-open set of arbitrary odd
functions, and for every odd zonal function plus a linear function.
\end{abstract}

\subjclass[2020]{52A20, 05C50, 15A69, 55M25}
\keywords{Makeev conjecture, root system $A_d$, constant width, combinatorial Hodge decomposition, tensor diagonalization, Brouwer degree}

\maketitle

\section{Introduction}

Makeev's universal-cover conjecture asks whether every body of constant width
can be circumscribed by a suitable copy of the dual difference body of a
regular simplex; see Makeev~\cite{Makeev1992}.  Kuperberg translated the
problem into an odd-function interpolation problem on the $A_d$ root system,
proved the resulting assertion in dimension three, and showed that the
Euler-class count used there vanishes in higher dimensions
\cite{Kuperberg1999}.  The vanishing is inconclusive: it neither produces nor
rules out zeros of the special test maps obtained from one scalar function.
Related Makeev-type interpolation and universal-cover questions continue to
be studied; compare Karasev~\cite{Karasev2016} and Chen~\cite{Chen2026}.

This note is a streamlined reorganization of the supplied proof.  Standard
literature is used for the background mechanisms: the cut--cycle
orthogonal decomposition is the complete-graph instance of combinatorial
Hodge theory~\cite{JiangLimYaoYe2011}; the cubic variational argument is close
in spirit to orthogonal tensor diagonalization~\cite{MartinVanLoan2008}; and
the local stability result is a routine application of Brouwer degree
\cite[Chapter~1]{Deimling1985}.  No cited theorem replaces the explicit
algebraic transversality calculation in dimension four, so that calculation
is retained in Appendix~\ref{app:algebra}.

The main result is the following.

\begin{theorem}[Dimension-four counterexample]\label{thm:main}
There is $\eps_0>0$ such that, for every real $\eps$ with
$0<|\eps|<\eps_0$, the smooth odd function
\[
 f_\eps(z_1,z_2)
 =\Rea(z_1^2\overline{z_2})
  +\eps |z_1|^2\Ima(z_1^2\overline{z_2}),
 \qquad (z_1,z_2)\in S^3\subset\C^2,
\]
has no $A\in\SO(4)$ and $b\in\R^4$ satisfying
\[
 f_\eps(Au_{ij})=b\cdot Au_{ij}
 \qquad(0\le i<j\le4).
\]
Consequently the proposed $A_d$ interpolation assertion is false already for
$d=4$.
\end{theorem}

A harmonic refinement, Corollary~\ref{cor:harmonic-counterexample}, shows
that spherical-harmonic degrees three and five already suffice.

\section{Exact edge labels and the test map}\label{sec:testmap}

Put $m=d+1$ and
\[
 V=\one^\perp\subset\R^m,
 \qquad
 u_{ij}=\frac{e_i-e_j}{\sqrt2}\in S(V)
 \quad(0\le i<j\le d).
\]
The normalization is essential because the function is evaluated on the unit
sphere.

Let $\cE$ be the space of skew edge matrices
$y=(y_{ij})_{0\le i,j\le d}$, with inner product
\[
 \inner{x}{y}_{\cE}=\sum_{i<j}x_{ij}y_{ij}.
\]
For $c\in V$ set
\[
 (\delta c)_{ij}=\frac{c_i-c_j}{\sqrt2}.
\]
These are exactly the restrictions of linear functionals on $V$ to the
normalized roots.  Let
\[
 \cC=\{X\in\R^{m\times m}:X^T=-X,\ X\one=0\}.
\]
Extending a skew operator on $V$ by zero on $\R\one$ identifies
$\cC$ with $\so(V)$.

\begin{lemma}[Exact labels; complete-graph Hodge decomposition]
\label{lem:exact}
For $y\in\cE$, the following are equivalent.
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item $y=\delta c$ for some $c\in V$;
\item $y_{ij}+y_{jk}+y_{ki}=0$ for all distinct $i,j,k$;
\item $\inner{X}{y}_{\cE}=0$ for every $X\in\cC$.
\end{enumerate}
If $Y=(y_{ij})$ and
$\Pi=I-m^{-1}\one\one^T$, these are also equivalent to
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Pi-criterion}
 \Pi Y\Pi=0.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The implication (i)$\Rightarrow$(ii) is telescoping.  Conversely, assume
(ii), set $c_0=0$ and $c_i=\sqrt2\,y_{i0}$, and use the triangle $(i,j,0)$
to obtain $y_{ij}=(c_i-c_j)/\sqrt2$.  Subtracting the mean of the $c_i$
places $c$ in $V$.

For $X^T=-X$,
\[
 \sum_{i<j}X_{ij}(c_i-c_j)=\sum_i c_i\sum_jX_{ij}.
\]
Thus $\operatorname{im}\delta\perp\cC$.  The two spaces have complementary
dimensions, $m-1$ and $\binom m2-(m-1)$, proving (iii).
Finally, $\Pi Y\Pi=0$ is equivalent to
$Y=\rho\one^T-\one\rho^T$ for some $\rho$, hence to
$y_{ij}=\rho_i-\rho_j$; this is (i) after putting
$c_i=\sqrt2\rho_i$ and subtracting the mean.  This is the cut--cycle
specialization of the graph Hodge decomposition
\cite{JiangLimYaoYe2011}.
\end{proof}

For an odd continuous $f\colon S(V)\to\R$ define
\[
 y^f(A)_{ij}=f(Au_{ij}),
 \qquad
 \cT_f(A)=\proj_{\cC}y^f(A),
 \qquad A\in\SO(V).
\]

\begin{corollary}[Test-map formulation]\label{cor:testmap}
The required interpolation property holds for $f$ if and only if
$\cT_f(A)=0$ for some $A\in\SO(V)$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
If $\cT_f(A)=0$, Lemma~\ref{lem:exact} gives $c\in V$ with
$f(Au_{ij})=c\cdot u_{ij}$.  Taking $b=Ac$ gives
$c\cdot u_{ij}=b\cdot Au_{ij}$.  The converse is immediate.
\end{proof}

\section{The cubic gradient identity}\label{sec:cubic}

Define the distinguished cubic
\[
 p(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{d}x_i^3,
 \qquad x\in V.
\]
For a homogeneous cubic $Q$, let $T_Q$ be its symmetric trilinear
polarization, extended to $\R^m$ by orthogonal projection of each argument to
$V$, and use the invariant tensor inner product
\[
 \inner{Q}{R}=\sum_{a,b,c=0}^{d}(T_Q)_{abc}(T_R)_{abc}.
\]
The action is $(g\cdot Q)(x)=Q(g^{-1}x)$, and
$X\cdot Q=\left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_{0}(e^{tX}\cdot Q)$.

\begin{lemma}[Cubic edge identity]\label{lem:cubic-identity}
For every homogeneous cubic $Q$ on $V$ and every $X\in\cC$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:cubic-identity}
 \inner{Q}{X\cdot p}
 =2\sqrt2\sum_{i<j}X_{ij}Q(u_{ij}).
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Since
\[
 (X\cdot p)(x)=-3\sum_{i,j}X_{ij}x_i^2x_j,
\]
we have
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tensor-side}
 \inner{Q}{X\cdot p}=-3\sum_{i,j}X_{ij}(T_Q)_{iij}.
\end{equation}
Expanding $Q(e_i-e_j)$ and summing against $X_{ij}$, the pure diagonal
terms vanish because $X\one=0$, while skew-symmetry gives
\[
 \sum_{i,j}X_{ij}(T_Q)_{ijj}
 =-\sum_{i,j}X_{ij}(T_Q)_{iij}.
\]
Therefore
\[
 \sum_{i<j}X_{ij}Q(e_i-e_j)
 =-3\sum_{i,j}X_{ij}(T_Q)_{iij}.
\]
Homogeneity and $e_i-e_j=\sqrt2\,u_{ij}$ yield
\eqref{eq:cubic-identity}.
\end{proof}

For a cubic $P$ define the height function
\[
 \Phi_P(A)=\inner{P}{A\cdot p},
 \qquad A\in\SO(V).
\]
Identifying $T_A\SO(V)$ with $A\cC$ by the curve $Ae^{tX}$ gives the
central gradient formula
\begin{equation}\label{eq:gradient}
 \boxed{
 d\Phi_P(A)[AX]
 =2\sqrt2\,\inner{\cT_P(A)}{X}_{\cE}.}
\end{equation}
Indeed, apply Lemma~\ref{lem:cubic-identity} to
$A^{-1}\cdot P$, noting that $(A^{-1}\cdot P)(u_{ij})=P(Au_{ij})$.
Thus the cycle defect of a cubic is, up to a constant, the gradient of a
height function on the orthogonal orbit of $p$.  Maximizing related diagonal
contractions is a standard theme in orthogonal tensor decomposition; see
\cite{MartinVanLoan2008}.

\begin{theorem}[Odd cubics plus linear functions]\label{thm:cubics}
Let $d\ge2$.  If
\[
 f=P+\ell\quad\text{on }S(V),
\]
where $P$ is homogeneous cubic and $\ell$ is linear, then there are
$A\in\SO(V)$ and $b\in V$ such that
$f(Au_{ij})=b\cdot Au_{ij}$ for every $i<j$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The compact group $\SO(V)$ contains a critical point $A$ of $\Phi_P$.
Equation~\eqref{eq:gradient} gives $\cT_P(A)=0$, and
Corollary~\ref{cor:testmap} supplies a linear functional matching $P$ on the
rotated roots.  A linear summand is already exact at every rotation and can
be added to that functional.
\end{proof}

\section{Two further positive results}\label{sec:positive}

\subsection{A $C^0$-open set of arbitrary odd functions}

\begin{theorem}[Uniform stability near $p$]\label{thm:stability}
For every $d\ge2$ there is $\eta_d>0$ such that every continuous odd
$f\colon S(V)\to\R$ satisfying
$\|f-p\|_\infty<\eta_d$ has the interpolation property.
The same holds near every nonzero scalar multiple or rotation of $p$, and
adding an arbitrary linear function does not affect the conclusion.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
First, $p(u_{ij})=0$, hence $\cT_p(I)=0$.  Let
$X\in\cC=\so(V)$.  For $u=u_{ij}$,
\[
 dp_u(Xu)=\frac32\bigl((Xu)_i+(Xu)_j\bigr)
          =-\frac3{\sqrt2}X_{ij}.
\]
The resulting edge matrix is already in $\cC$, so
\begin{equation}\label{eq:derivative-p}
 D\cT_p(I)[X]=-\frac3{\sqrt2}X.
\end{equation}
Thus $I$ is a nondegenerate zero.  Its local Brouwer degree is nonzero and
persists under sufficiently small uniform perturbations; see
\cite[Chapter~1]{Deimling1985}.  More explicitly, if
$N=\binom{d+1}{2}$, then
\[
 \sup_A\|\cT_f(A)-\cT_p(A)\|
 \le \sqrt N\,\|f-p\|_\infty.
\]
Choose a small exponential-coordinate ball around $I$ on whose boundary
$\cT_p$ is nonzero.  The displayed estimate and homotopy invariance of degree
show that $\cT_f$ has a zero in the ball whenever $\|f-p\|_\infty$ is small
enough.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Zonal functions}

\begin{theorem}[Odd zonal functions]\label{thm:zonal}
Let $d\ge2$, $a\in S(V)$, and let $h\colon[-1,1]\to\R$ be continuous and
odd.  Every function
\[
 f(x)=h(a\cdot x)+\ell(x),
\]
with $\ell$ linear, has the interpolation property.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
It is enough to take $\ell=0$.  Choose a nontrivial partition
$\{0,\dots,d\}=S\sqcup T$, with $s=|S|$, $t=|T|$, and $s+t=m$.  Put
\[
 c_i=\begin{cases}
 \alpha=\sqrt{\dfrac{t}{sm}},&i\in S,\\[2mm]
 \beta=-\sqrt{\dfrac{s}{tm}},&i\in T.
 \end{cases}
\]
Then $c\in S(V)$.  Choose $A\in\SO(V)$ with $A^Ta=c$.  The values
$a\cdot Au_{ij}=(c_i-c_j)/\sqrt2$ are $0$ on edges within one part and
$\pm\kappa$ across the partition, where
$\kappa=(\alpha-\beta)/\sqrt2>0$.  Since $h$ is odd, the labels are $0$ on
within-part edges and $\pm h(\kappa)$ on cross-edges.  They are exact: take
$z_i=\sqrt2h(\kappa)$ on $S$ and $z_i=0$ on $T$, then subtract the mean.
Thus $f(Au_{ij})=z\cdot u_{ij}=(Az)\cdot Au_{ij}$.
\end{proof}
